For a company whose post-SPAC balance sheet held roughly $306 million, the prepayment also constituted meaningful non-dilutive capital, signalling that one of the world's most creditworthy infrastructure operators was prepared to underwrite Oklo's development risk with real money.

## Switch and the 12-Gigawatt Master Agreement

The Equinix precedent framed what followed, but was dwarfed by what Switch and Oklo announced on 18 December 2024. Under a non-binding Master Power Agreement, the two companies outlined a framework for deploying up to 12 gigawatts of Aurora powerhouses at Switch's US data-centre campuses through 2044 — binding PPAs to follow as project milestones were reached. Switch chief executive Rob Roy described the rationale plainly:

> "The relationship with Oklo underscores our commitment to deploying advanced nuclear power at a transformative scale for our data centers."

DeWitte cast it in the language of the AI electricity thesis:

> "Rob Roy and the Switch team share the vision we have for nuclear energy's role in powering artificial intelligence and providing energy abundance."

The 12 GW figure was arresting against the broader SMR landscape. Before the Switch agreement, [Oklo's disclosed pipeline](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2024/Oklo-Secures-Partnerships-for-Up-to-750-Megawatts-of-Power-for-U.S.-Data-Centers/default.aspx) stood at approximately 2,100 megawatts — itself a tripling since the July 2023 SPAC announcement, encompassing the Equinix deal, a November 2024 pair of letters of intent for up to 750 megawatts combined with two unnamed data-centre operators, and a 100-megawatt LOI with Prometheus Hyperscale, a Nevada-based campus developer. Switch appended 12 GW in a single announcement. The aggregate required sustained qualification: reaching that volume by 2044 would imply several hundred individual Aurora units, each requiring its own NRC licence, construction campaign, and discrete HALEU fuel procurement — assumptions that compress a generation of project execution into a two-decade timeline.

## Industrial Customers: Oil and Gas, Distributed Power

Parallel to the data-centre push, Oklo targeted distributed industrial customers for whom grid unreliability and carbon-reduction mandates created overlapping procurement pressure. On [8 April 2024](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2024/Oklo-Signs-LOI-to-Supply-50-Megawatts-of-Power-to-Diamondback-Energy/default.aspx), the company disclosed a non-binding 50-megawatt LOI with Diamondback Energy for a 20-year power purchase arrangement — with renewal options for a further 20 years — covering oilfield operations conducted by Diamondback E&P LLC near Midland, Texas. The Aurora units would supply Permian Basin production sites ill-served by ERCOT's constrained western transmission margins. DeWitte framed the engagement in terms of the off-grid use case:

> "By developing and providing a low-cost, high-reliability, and emission-free energy source, Oklo is poised to help meet the growing energy requirements of operators like Diamondback."

The industrial thesis was reinforced in July 2025 by an alliance with [Liberty Energy](https://www.powermag.com/nuclear-developer-oklo-advances-dual-alliances-targeting-data-center-and-industrial-power-needs/), under which Liberty's Forte natural-gas generation platform would provide dispatchable power at energy-intensive sites in the near term while Aurora units progressed through licensing — a bridging structure designed to capture customers ahead of Oklo's commercial delivery window.

## The Department of Defense: Eielson Air Force Base

Aurora's small-footprint design found its starkest strategic application in the US military's formal selection of Oklo for a microreactor deployment at [Eielson Air Force Base](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2025/Oklo-Selected-as-Intended-Awardee-to-Provide-Clean-Reliable-Power-to-Eielson-Air-Force-Base-in-Alaska/default.aspx), Alaska. On 11 June 2025, the Defense Logistics Agency Energy issued a Notice of Intent to Award to Oklo on behalf of the Department of the Air Force and the broader DoD, for a 5-megawatt Aurora powerhouse at the installation under a proposed 30-year firm-fixed-price power purchase arrangement — a design-build-own-operate structure that kept capital expenditure off the government's balance sheet. Eielson, home of the 354th Fighter Wing, was selected partly because winter temperatures below −50°C drive extreme fuel costs and expose critical infrastructure to diesel supply-chain failure. The FY2019 National Defence Authorisation Act had mandated a functioning military microreactor by the end of 2027; the Eielson selection set Oklo on the path to satisfying that mandate. DeWitte said the award "reflects continued confidence in Oklo's ability to deliver clean and secure energy solutions for mission-critical infrastructure."

## NRC Licensing: From January 2022 Denial to the May 2026 PDC Milestone

Oklo's regulatory history tracked a five-year arc from setback to incremental validation. The company submitted the [NRC's first-ever non-light-water-reactor combined licence application](https://www.nrc.gov/reactors/new-reactors/large-lwr/col/aurora-oklo) in March 2020, targeting a 1.5-MWe demonstration unit at Idaho National Laboratory. On 6 January 2022 the Commission denied the application without prejudice, citing Oklo's repeated failure to supply adequate responses to requests for additional information concerning maximum credible accident methodology, safety classification of structures, systems, and components, and quality assurance programme description. The denial was a documentation deficiency ruling, not a technical veto on the reactor concept.

Oklo relaunched its NRC engagement in September 2022 with a new Licensing Project Plan structuring pre-application interactions. By [17 July 2025](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2025/Oklo-Advances-Licensing-with-Completion-of-NRC-Readiness-Assessment/default.aspx), the NRC had completed a Phase 1 readiness assessment of the refreshed Aurora-INL combined licence application — reviewing siting, safety analysis, component classification, and the QA programme — and identified no significant gaps that would prevent application acceptance. DeWitte called it "a productive engagement tool that moves our licensing and permitting work forward."

A more consequential milestone followed on [6 May 2026](https://oklo.com/newsroom/news-details/2026/Oklos-NRC-Principal-Design-Criteria-Topical-Report-Approved-for-Aurora-Powerhouse-in-Idaho/default.aspx), seventeen days before this chapter's frozen snapshot date. The NRC approved Oklo's Principal Design Criteria topical report for the Aurora powerhouse — the foundational document establishing the safety, reliability, and performance requirements that anchor the reactor's licence basis. The PDC approval was completed in less than half the agency's traditional review timeline, reflecting NRC modernisation efforts aligned with the federal ADVANCE Act. Approved PDC documents can be referenced directly in future submissions, eliminating repetitive review. DeWitte acknowledged: "Performance-based licensing, clear criteria, and efficient reviews are important to advancing modern nuclear projects safely and responsibly."

## HALEU: The Fuel-Cycle Bottleneck

Every milestone in Oklo's customer pipeline carried a single critical dependency: a domestic supply of high-assay low-enriched uranium that, as of the snapshot date, did not exist at commercial scale in the United States. Aurora's metallic fuel — a uranium-zirconium alloy enriched to between 10 and 20 percent U-235, far above the sub-5-percent standard for conventional light-water reactor fuel — had historically been produced at industrial scale only in Russia and China.

The structural constraint sharpened acutely in May 2024 when Congress enacted a [ban on imports of Russian enriched uranium](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/congress-passes-russian-uranium-import-ban-haleu-nuclear-fuel-advanced-reactors/715256/), closing the most immediately accessible HALEU supply route. The legislation simultaneously unlocked $2.7 billion in DOE production commitments, which the agency subsequently distributed in [three awards of $900 million each](https://www.powermag.com/doe-issues-2-7b-orders-to-scale-domestic-nuclear-leu-and-haleu-enrichment/) to Centrus Energy, General Matter, and Orano Federal Services for domestic enrichment capacity expansion over the following decade.

Oklo's primary supply relationship ran through [Centrus Energy](https://www.centrusenergy.com/news/oklo-and-centrus-energy-sign-memorandum-of-understanding-for-fuel-components-and-power-procurement-to-support-the-deployment-of-advanced-fission-technologies-in-southern-ohio/) (NYSE: LEU) and its American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio — the only NRC-licensed HALEU production facility in the United States. A memorandum of understanding signed on 28 August 2023 covered HALEU supply to Oklo, component manufacturing at Centrus's Oak Ridge facility, and a reciprocal arrangement under which Centrus would purchase electricity from two Aurora powerhouses planned at the Piketon campus to power the enrichment cascade itself. Centrus chief executive Daniel Poneman characterised the agreement as a closed loop: "We are excited to see strong support from industry leaders like Oklo as well as growing bipartisan support in Congress."

Centrus began operating its pilot centrifuge cascade in October 2023 and completed a first 20-kilogram delivery to the DOE in November of that year. By mid-2025, cumulative production had reached approximately [920 kilograms](https://www.powermag.com/centrus-completes-900-kg-haleu-delivery-to-doe-in-u-s-nuclear-fuel-enrichment-milestone/) — a meaningful demonstration of process viability while remaining several orders of magnitude below the tonnage that the Switch and Equinix pipelines would eventually require.

Oklo maintained a parallel recycled-fuel pathway at Idaho National Laboratory, where spent metallic material recovered from the Experimental Breeder Reactor II — the fast-sodium reactor from whose design heritage Aurora directly descends — was being processed at INL's Fuel Conditioning Facility into Aurora fuel feedstock under DOE agreement. In March 2026, the DOE Idaho Operations Office approved the [Nuclear Safety Design Agreement](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260317730831/en/Oklo-Announces-U.S.-Department-of-Energy-Approval-for-Nuclear-Safety-Design-Agreement-of-Aurora-Powerhouse-at-Idaho-National-Laboratory) for both the Aurora Powerhouse and its co-located Aurora Fuel Fabrication Facility at INL — formal design-safety approvals that brought the first commercial deployment, targeted for late 2027, a structural step closer to construction readiness. The fuel recycling pathway offered Oklo a near-term supply hedge that did not depend on the still-nascent domestic HALEU enrichment industry scaling fast enough to match the ambitions written into its LOI stack.

chapters.title: Where Oklo sits against NuScale, X-energy, TerraPower, Kairos, BWXT
chapters.body:
## The Listed Cohort

The US small modular reactor development landscape, as of May 2026, comprised roughly a dozen credible programmes spanning the full technology spectrum — light-water derivatives, high-temperature gas-cooled designs, sodium-fast-spectrum concepts, and at least one novel molten-salt storage hybrid. No commercial SMR had yet delivered a single kilowatt-hour for a paying customer on US soil. That shared pre-revenue condition obscured meaningful distinctions in technology readiness, commercial model, and addressable customer set that materially affected each developer's risk-return profile.

Of the listed US equities with material SMR exposure, only two offered clean pure-play positioning: Oklo (NYSE: OKLO) and NuScale Power (NYSE: SMR). BWX Technologies (NYSE: BWXT), the third listed name commonly cited alongside them, was principally an established nuclear services and US Navy propulsion contractor whose SMR product line, the BWRX-based microreactor variants, represented an emerging but not yet dominant share of its revenue base and market capitalisation.

NuScale was the cautionary data point for the sector. The Portland, Oregon-based company completed its own SPAC-era listing in 2022 and entered the snapshot period as Oklo's most direct comparable — the only other dedicated SMR developer with a public market price. Its 77 MW VOYGR pressurised-water-reactor module carried the distinction of being the first SMR design to receive NRC design certification, a milestone achieved in 2022. That regulatory head-start proved insufficient to rescue the company's flagship Carbon Free Power Project, the planned six-module installation at Idaho National Laboratory for the Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems cooperative, which was cancelled in November 2023 after per-module cost estimates escalated sharply from initial projections. The cancellation marked the most visible commercial setback in the SMR sector's modern history and weighed on NuScale's equity for the balance of 2024 and into 2025. The company subsequently refocused on international opportunities, including a project development agreement in Romania and a large letter of intent with Standard Power for US-based data centre load. NuScale's technology — a proven light-water fuel cycle with no requirement for high-assay low-enriched uranium — gave it a structural fuel supply advantage. Its commercial challenge was demonstrating that revised cost assumptions could underpin bankable project economics after the CFPP experience.

BWXT occupied a different position in the landscape. Its nuclear services backlog, anchored in long-duration US Navy contracts for submarine and carrier reactor components, gave it balance sheet stability that pure-play SMR developers lacked. The company's Generation IV SMR ambitions were real but deliberately paced against its existing industrial base. For investors assessing the AI-driven electricity demand thesis, BWXT offered nuclear sector exposure with substantially lower pre-commercial binary risk — and correspondingly less upside leverage to SMR deployment at scale.

## Private Developers: Gas, Sodium, and Light Water

Beyond the listed cohort, the US SMR landscape was populated by well-capitalised private developers whose programmes ranged from near-term to structurally longer-dated.

**X-energy** was among the most commercially advanced. Its Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, a pebble-bed design targeting approximately 80 MW per unit, had secured a Department of Energy Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program award and attracted a headline commercial commitment from Amazon, which announced an LOI in 2024 for multiple SMR plants. Dow Chemical was a second anchor customer, targeting industrial process heat applications at a Gulf Coast facility — a use case that distinguished X-energy from data centre-centric competitors. The HTGR's high outlet temperature (approximately 750°C) made it technically well-suited to industrial heat and hydrogen production, markets that Oklo's lower-temperature sodium design did not address.

**TerraPower**, founded by Bill Gates and backed partly by GE Hitachi, was developing the Natrium reactor — a sodium-fast-spectrum design paired with molten salt thermal storage capable of dispatching up to approximately 500 MW during peak demand periods from a roughly 345 MW reactor core. The Wyoming demonstration plant, sited at a retiring coal facility in Kemmerer, was the company's most concrete near-term milestone. Natrium's combination of fast-spectrum breeding potential and on-site storage differentiated it meaningfully from both light-water SMRs and Oklo's Aurora; its scale — comparable to a small conventional gas-peaker plant — also placed it in a different customer segment than Oklo's 15-to-75-MW range.

**Kairos Power** was advancing a fluoride salt-cooled high-temperature reactor (KP-FHR), with a demonstration project — Hermes — under construction at Oak Ridge, Tennessee under a DOE ARDP cost-share award. Kairos had signed a 500 MW LOI with Google in late 2023, one of the most prominent technology-company commitments to advanced nuclear at that stage of the sector's development. Its technology differed from Oklo's on nearly every axis: coolant chemistry, fuel form, temperature regime, and target application.

**GE Hitachi's BWRX-300**, a 300 MW boiling-water reactor SMR representing an evolutionary step from the licensed ESBWR design, was the furthest-advanced large-SMR design in North America by some metrics. Ontario Power Generation had selected the BWRX-300 for the Darlington New Nuclear Project in Canada, and the Tennessee Valley Authority was advancing a US deployment. The BWRX-300's light-water technology, established regulatory pathway through GE Hitachi's existing design certification heritage, and large module size positioned it as a more conventional utility procurement rather than a distributed-energy play.

**Westinghouse's AP300** completed the light-water cluster — a 300 MW derivative of the AP1000 that offered utilities a familiar technology path with lower first-of-a-kind engineering risk. **Holtec's SMR-300**, another pressurised-water design, rounded out the light-water SMR field.

## Three Differentiators — and One Constraint

Against this field, Oklo's competitive positioning rested on three claims that, taken together, amounted to a genuinely distinct market thesis.

| Developer | Technology | Module Size (MW) | Fuel | Commercial Model | Public / Private |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oklo | Sodium fast spectrum | 15–75 | HALEU + recycled | PPA ownership | Public (NYSE: OKLO) |
| NuScale | PWR (light water) | 77 | LEU | Reactor sale | Public (NYSE: SMR) |
| X-energy | HTGR (gas-cooled) | ~80 | TRISO/LEU | Reactor sale | Private |
| TerraPower | Sodium fast + molten salt | ~345 core / 500 dispatch | Metallic/HALEU | TBD | Private |
| GE Hitachi | BWR (light water) | 300 | LEU | Reactor sale | Private (JV) |
| Westinghouse | PWR (light water) | 300 | LEU | Reactor sale | Private |
| Kairos | FHR (fluoride salt) | ~140 | TRISO/LEU | Reactor sale | Private |
| Holtec | PWR (light water) | 300 | LEU | Reactor sale | Private |

*First*, plant scale. Aurora's 15-to-75-MW range sat below the floor of virtually every competing design. That was not merely a technical footnote — it opened customer segments inaccessible to 300 MW designs, including remote industrial installations, military bases (Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, was an early DOD commitment), Permian Basin operators such as Diamondback Energy, and hyperscale data centre campuses where modular incremental capacity additions were operationally preferable to single large-plant procurement. The 500 MW LOI signed with Equinix, the world's largest colocation operator, illustrated the thesis at scale: a 500 MW commitment could be satisfied with multiple Aurora modules deployed across distributed sites rather than a single centralised plant.

*Second*, commercial structure. Most competing developers — NuScale, GE Hitachi, Westinghouse — were pursuing a reactor-sale or engineering-procurement-construction model in which the utility or off-taker owned and operated the plant. Oklo's model was materially different: the company intended to own and operate its Aurora plants, selling electricity under long-term power purchase agreements. That structure inverted the revenue profile, transforming Oklo from an equipment manufacturer into an electricity producer — more akin to an independent power producer than a nuclear OEM. It also concentrated execution and operational risk on Oklo's balance sheet, but management argued it aligned incentives with customers and captured the full value of the energy produced over a reactor's operating life.

*Third*, sponsorship and strategic context. Sam Altman's chairmanship of AltC Acquisition Corp and continued board involvement post-merger gave Oklo a direct association with OpenAI and the broader AI infrastructure investment wave. That linkage was commercially and narratively significant: it positioned Aurora — a technology designed for off-grid industrial applications — as the preferred power supply for the AI data centre build-out at precisely the moment that hyperscalers were scrambling to secure firm, carbon-free baseload capacity. The Equinix and Switch LOIs were the tangible commercial expression of that thesis.

## The Strategic Question: Execution

The competitive distinctions above were real. The competitive risk was equally real, and its name was execution. NRC licensing for the Aurora combined license application remained an open process at the snapshot date, with no commercial plants in construction and no firm commissioning timeline. The HALEU fuel cycle, while technically coherent — Aurora's design could utilise both fresh HALEU and recycled spent nuclear fuel, a differentiated supply-side attribute — remained structurally constrained by limited US enrichment capacity following post-Russian-invasion import restrictions. Centrus Energy's American Centrifuge Plant at Piketon, Ohio represented the only domestic HALEU production facility at pilot scale.

Competitors dependent on conventional low-enriched uranium faced no such supply bottleneck. NuScale, GE Hitachi, Westinghouse, and Holtec could draw on established commercial enrichment markets. X-energy's TRISO fuel required its own specialised supply chain, but was distinct from HALEU's enrichment-capacity ceiling. TerraPower, as the only other sodium-fast developer among the principal US competitors, shared Oklo's HALEU exposure — a structural parallel worth noting given TerraPower's substantially larger reactor scale and deeper DOE programme integration.

Customer LOI conversion remained the second execution variable. A letter of intent is not a power purchase agreement, and no Oklo LOI had yet converted to a binding commercial contract within the snapshot window. The Equinix commitment for 500 MW was significant as a statement of intent from a counterparty with both the capital and the operational need to absorb large quantities of clean firm power. Whether that translated to signed, financed project agreements would depend on NRC licensing progress, HALEU supply certainty, and Aurora's demonstrated construction cost structure — none of which were resolved facts as of May 2026.

The competitive landscape Oklo was navigating, in sum, was wide, well-capitalised, and technologically diverse. Its differentiation was structural rather than incremental. The bear case was not that competitors were better-positioned in Oklo's specific niche; it was that Oklo's specific niche might take longer to reach than the equity's implied timeline. Licensing, fuel, and financing risk were not unique to Oklo in the SMR sector, but they fell with particular weight on a company whose entire commercial programme depended on a first-of-kind reactor design reaching construction, commissioning, and operational status without the benefit of a predecessor plant.

chapters.title: From 2022 NRC denial through SPAC, Equinix LOI, and ongoing licensing
chapters.body:
## The January 2022 rejection and what it forced

The document that defined Oklo's next several years arrived in the opening days of 2022. On 3 January, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission formally denied, without prejudice, the company's combined licence application for an Aurora demonstration powerhouse at Idaho National Laboratory — making Oklo the first advanced-reactor developer in the modern NRC era to receive a formal licence denial on a combined licence application.

The rejection was not a safety finding against Aurora. The NRC's review identified deficiencies across several technical areas: the adequacy of the accident-source-term analysis, the completeness of the fuel-qualification data package, and the sufficiency of the application's treatment of several design-basis conditions. "Without prejudice" carried legal significance — Oklo retained the right to resubmit — but the regulatory arithmetic was unambiguous. The application as submitted had not met the NRC's information completeness standards, and the agency had declined to continue the review.

The denial landed at a company that was, at that point, still privately held, nine years from founding, and operating on venture and Department of Energy grant capital with no commercial revenue. Jacob DeWitte and Caroline Cochran had co-founded Oklo in 2013 while both were pursuing graduate work at MIT, with DeWitte completing his doctorate in nuclear science and engineering. They had drawn on the Experimental Breeder Reactor II heritage at Idaho National Laboratory — a sodium-cooled fast reactor that had operated for three decades at the INL site — to design Aurora, a compact metallic-fuelled fast-spectrum plant configurable between 15 and 75 megawatts for commercial deployments. Y Combinator had backed the company in 2014, placing it among the handful of advanced-reactor startups to emerge from the US university ecosystem in that era with institutional support early in their development.

The NRC pre-application engagement had run from approximately 2018 through 2021. The January 2022 denial reflected the structural difficulty of applying existing NRC licensing frameworks to a reactor design with no commercial precedent in the modern regulatory environment. Oklo responded by beginning work on a revised application that would address the identified deficiencies — a process that would require additional fuel qualification data and more complete accident-analysis documentation.

## The AltC merger announcement and the Equinix signal

Eighteen months after the NRC denial, the company's trajectory shifted materially. In July 2023, Oklo announced it had agreed to merge with AltC Acquisition Corp, a special-purpose acquisition company sponsored by Sam Altman — then and now the chief executive of OpenAI — who served as AltC's chairman. The transaction valued Oklo at approximately $850 million on a post-merger basis.

Altman's involvement carried significance that extended beyond the capital structure. By mid-2023, the AI data centre electricity demand thesis had become one of the organising narratives in US energy and technology investment. Hyperscalers and cloud infrastructure operators were beginning to examine nuclear power as the only zero-carbon generation source capable of delivering the combination of power density, capacity factor, and grid independence that large-scale AI compute required. Altman's chairmanship of a nuclear SMR developer — while simultaneously running OpenAI, whose compute requirements were among the most visible proxies for the broader demand inflection — made the strategic logic explicit rather than inferential.

Announced concurrently with the AltC merger, a letter of intent from Equinix, the global data centre operator, for 500 megawatts of Aurora-derived power capacity provided the first large-scale commercial validation of the demand thesis. Equinix's global data centre footprint and the scale of the commitment signalled that at least one major infrastructure operator was treating Aurora as a credible future power source rather than speculative technology. Letters of intent carry no binding obligation, and the 500 MW figure implied multiple Aurora deployments across several years — but the commercial signal was among the largest made by any hyperscaler-adjacent operator toward any single SMR developer at that stage.

## SPAC close and the customer pipeline build

The AltC-Oklo business combination closed on 9 May 2024, listing Oklo on the New York Stock Exchange and providing the company with public-market capital for its pre-commercial development programme. The post-merger period brought additional customer LOI announcements that extended the pipeline beyond the data centre sector.

Switch, a data centre operator, signed a letter of intent for Aurora power capacity. Wyoming Energy Authority formalised a commitment representing broader state-level engagement. Diamondback Energy, the Permian Basin oil and gas producer, signed an LOI reflecting industrial demand for off-grid power in remote locations where grid access is constrained and natural gas is the dominant but increasingly cost-variable alternative. The United States Air Force selected Oklo for a demonstration deployment at Eielson Air Force Base in Alaska, providing DoD validation and a funded pathway toward a first operational plant on federal government property.

| Customer | Sector | Announced LOI scope |
|---|---|---|
| Equinix | Data centre / colocation | 500 MW |
| Switch | Data centre | Undisclosed MW |
| Wyoming Energy Authority | State government / industrial | Undisclosed |
| Diamondback Energy | Oil and gas, Permian Basin | Undisclosed |
| Eielson Air Force Base | US Department of Defense | Demonstration deployment |

The customer slate represented a deliberate diversification across end-market segments — data centre, industrial, remote federal — consistent with the Aurora's design flexibility across the 15-to-75-megawatt configuration range. None of the letters of intent constituted binding contracts, and the gap between LOI commitments and executed power purchase agreements with construction milestones remained the central commercial risk the company carried into the post-SPAC period.

## The board transition and Altman's departure from the chair

In April 2025, Sam Altman stepped down from Oklo's chairmanship. Lieutenant General John Jansen, United States Air Force retired, succeeded him as board chairman. The transition was characterised by the company as planned succession. Altman remained associated with Oklo through his investment relationship, but his departure from the chairmanship reflected the increasingly complex potential conflict-of-interest dynamics that arose as OpenAI's compute infrastructure demands grew — and as OpenAI's electricity procurement strategies became subjects of public scrutiny in the context of its partnership discussions with utility and nuclear-power providers.

Jansen's appointment brought defence-industry and Air Force operational pedigree to the chairmanship at a moment when the Eielson AFB deployment represented one of Oklo's clearest near-term commercial pathways. Michael Klein, the SPAC sponsor partner who had led the AltC transaction, remained on the board, providing institutional continuity through the post-merger period.

## Ongoing NRC licensing and forward catalysts

The NRC combined licence application for the first Aurora plant at Idaho National Laboratory remained under review as of the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026. The review process for advanced reactor designs under the NRC's framework — whether the traditional Part 52 combined licence pathway or the new Part 53 advanced-reactor framework that the agency finalised in 2024 — involves iterative requests for additional information, design-basis confirmations, and safety evaluation work that has historically extended over multi-year timelines even for more conventional reactor designs.

Oklo's licensing trajectory carried several structural dependencies. High-assay low-enriched uranium, the fuel type Aurora requires, remained subject to constrained US domestic enrichment capacity following the legislative restriction on Russian-sourced HALEU. The DOE's domestic HALEU enrichment programme and Centrus Energy's American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio, represented the principal near-term US supply pathway, but volumes available for commercial SMR deployment remained limited relative to the pipeline of developers competing for allocation.

Forward catalysts from the snapshot date included an NRC decision on the Aurora-INL combined licence application; a potential construction permit authorisation at the INL site; additional customer LOI conversions to binding contracts or power purchase agreements; HALEU fuel supply commitments adequate to support a first-plant construction timeline; and potential equity or debt capital raises to extend the development runway into commercial operation.

## Specialist commentary framing

Specialist commentary framing of Oklo by Aleabit was not surfaced in the bounded primary-source set.

Among broader market observers, the prevailing analytical tension through 2025 and into 2026 centred on the gap between the equity market's willingness to price Oklo's customer pipeline and licensing optionality at a substantial premium to net asset value, and the binary regulatory and construction-execution risks that would determine whether Aurora's first plant produced commercial power on a timeline relevant to the data centre electricity demand cycle. Bull-case framing emphasised the uniqueness of Aurora's fast-reactor design heritage, the quality of the customer LOI pipeline, and the structural scarcity of investable pure-play SMR equities at public-market scale. Bear-case framing noted the absence of binding contracts, the HALEU supply constraint, the NRC licensing uncertainty following the 2022 denial, and the competitive pressure from the broader advanced-reactor developer set — NuScale, X-energy, TerraPower, Kairos Power, and BWXT among them — each pursuing parallel licensing and commercial timelines. The resolution of those competing framings remained contingent, as of 23 May 2026, on regulatory and commercial milestones that had not yet materialised.

chapters.title: Sodium-fast reactor IP, HALEU fuel cycle, and NRC Part 53 licensing
chapters.body:
## A reactor born in the Idaho desert

The technical lineage of the Aurora powerhouse runs directly to a squat concrete building on the eastern Snake River Plain, where the Experimental Breeder Reactor II operated for thirty years before the Department of Energy shut it down in 1994. EBR-II was a sodium-cooled, metal-fuelled fast reactor that generated 62.5 MWt — enough electricity to power the Idaho National Laboratory campus — and, crucially, demonstrated something that would later become central to Oklo's investor pitch: inherent passive safety without operator action or emergency cooling systems.

In April 1986, INL engineers deliberately disabled EBR-II's control rods and cooling pumps simultaneously. The reactor shut itself down through physics alone, its metallic fuel expanding as temperatures rose, reducing neutron flux and quenching the fission reaction. That test, run twice in a single day, produced data that Jacob DeWitte and Caroline Cochran would draw on when they co-founded Oklo in Cambridge, Massachusetts in 2013, both holding MIT degrees in nuclear science and engineering. DeWitte had spent time at INL; Cochran brought reactor physics expertise. Together they licensed the EBR-II operational knowledge base from the DOE and set about miniaturising it into a commercial product.

## The Aurora architecture

The Aurora powerhouse is a compact, factory-assembled fast-spectrum reactor designed to ship to site and operate with minimal on-site staffing. Oklo has publicly described three plant configurations — nominally 15 MW, 50 MW, and 75 MW of thermal output — though its initial licensing work centred on a demonstration unit at the lower end of that range. The core physics are unchanged across configurations: metallic uranium-zirconium fuel rods sit in a sodium coolant pool; fast neutrons sustain the chain reaction; the absence of a moderator keeps the neutron spectrum hard, enabling fuel breeding and ultimately the possibility of running on recycled spent fuel.

The metallic fuel is central to both the safety case and the IP strategy. Uranium-zirconium alloy has a strongly negative temperature coefficient — as the fuel heats, reactivity drops. Combined with the thermal mass of the sodium pool and a natural convection cooling loop, the design aims to achieve what Oklo's filings describe as "walk-away safe" shutdown characteristics derived directly from the EBR-II heritage. The company has filed patents covering the fuel composition, the fuel fabrication process, and the integration of the fuel assembly with the reactor vessel geometry, building a defensive portfolio around the specific adaptation of EBR-II know-how to a modular commercial form factor.

Sodium as a coolant carries well-understood engineering constraints. It reacts violently with water and burns in air, demanding sealed primary loops, inert-gas cover systems, and specialised maintenance procedures. Oklo's design addresses this partly through the pool configuration — the reactor vessel itself serves as the primary containment for the sodium inventory — and partly through reduced operating pressure. Unlike pressurised-water reactors, sodium-cooled systems run near atmospheric pressure, eliminating the large-break loss-of-coolant accident scenario that dominates PWR safety analysis. The operational IP around sodium handling, leak detection, and sodium fire suppression represents a distinct body of knowledge that Oklo has sought to protect and that, in practice, constitutes a meaningful barrier to replication by new entrants without access to comparable operational heritage.

## HALEU and the fuel cycle

Aurora runs on high-assay low-enriched uranium — HALEU, enriched between five and twenty percent in the fissile U-235 isotope, compared with the three-to-five percent typical of commercial light-water-reactor fuel. The higher enrichment density allows the compact core geometry that makes the Aurora modular and transportable; it also means the fuel cycle sits in a regulatory and supply-chain space that is structurally more constrained than conventional nuclear.

Oklo's fuel cycle IP extends beyond the reactor core itself. The company holds intellectual property covering fuel fabrication methods for metallic HALEU fuel, processes for handling and processing recycled spent metallic fuel, and the broader operational envelope for fuel management in a fast-spectrum sodium environment. The recycled-fuel ambition — using spent fuel from light-water reactors as a feedstock after pyroprocessing — was central to Oklo's original founding thesis and remains part of its long-term commercial narrative, even if the near-term licensing pathway focuses on fresh HALEU.

The HALEU supply chain represents a structural risk that Oklo shares with the broader advanced reactor sector. As of the snapshot date, Centrus Energy operated the only US commercial HALEU production facility, a cascade at its American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio, authorised by a 2022 DOE contract. Russian enricher TENEX had historically been a significant HALEU source; congressional action culminating in the 2024 Russian uranium import ban effectively closed that channel. DOE has pursued emergency HALEU production contracting to bridge the gap, but declared production capacity remains well below what a scaled Aurora deployment would require. Oklo's fuel supply strategy, as disclosed in its SEC filings, relies on a combination of DOE downblending of existing government HALEU stocks and commercial enrichment contracts, with the long-term intent of integrating its own fuel fabrication capability.

## NRC Part 53 and the licensing trajectory

The regulatory pathway for Aurora has been the defining operational challenge of the company's first decade. Oklo submitted its first combined license application to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in March 2020, targeting a demonstration Aurora at INL. In January 2022, the NRC formally docketed a denial of that application, citing insufficient information across several safety analysis areas including fuel performance, accident source terms, and the methodology for demonstrating compliance. The denial was a setback but not a fatality; it produced a detailed record of NRC staff concerns that the company subsequently used to structure its revised application work.

The more significant regulatory development was the maturation of NRC Part 53 — formally titled the "Technology-Inclusive, Risk-Informed, and Performance-Based" licensing framework, or TIRPB. Developed over several years in response to congressional direction in the Nuclear Energy Innovation and Modernization Act of 2019, Part 53 was designed to accommodate advanced reactor designs that do not fit the light-water-reactor assumptions embedded in Part 52, the existing combined-license pathway. The NRC published the final Part 53 rule in July 2024. The framework introduces a performance-based safety approach, permitting applicants to demonstrate safety through probabilistic risk assessment and functional requirements rather than prescriptive design-basis accident catalogues derived from LWR experience.

Oklo has structured its revised licensing work around Part 53, a choice that aligns the Aurora's inherent-safety argument — passive shutdown, low-pressure operation, walk-away characteristics — with a regulatory methodology that can in principle credit those characteristics without forcing them into an LWR analytical mould. The revised combined license application, when filed, will be among the first submissions under the new framework, meaning Oklo and the NRC are co-developing the practical interpretation of Part 53 in real time.

> "We're not trying to make a light-water reactor. We're trying to bring forward a fundamentally different technology, and the regulatory framework needs to reflect that," DeWitte said in remarks to the Nuclear Energy Institute's annual conference, as reported by [Power Magazine](https://www.powermag.com).

The DOE's site agreement at INL provides the physical location for that first application — a parcel on the same campus where EBR-II once operated, granting the demonstration plant both symbolic continuity and practical proximity to the fuel cycle infrastructure and operational expertise concentrated at the national laboratory. Whether the NRC review clock under Part 53 can align with Oklo's customer delivery commitments — particularly the Equinix 500 MW letter of intent and the Eielson Air Force Base demonstration — remains the central execution variable for the investment case.

chapters.title: NRC licensing, HALEU supply, LOI-to-revenue conversion, capital raise need
chapters.body:
## The Six-Layer Risk Stack

Five dependencies must align sequentially — regulatory, fuel, contract, construction, and capital — before Oklo collects its first dollar of revenue. Each carries its own probability of delay or failure; in combination, they constitute a compound risk profile that distinguishes Oklo from virtually every other listed energy equity. Understanding that profile, layer by layer, is the essential work of any serious investor analysis.

## NRC Licensing: A New Framework, a Prior Denial

The most foundational risk is regulatory. Oklo's first Aurora plant — targeted at Idaho National Laboratory's Materials and Fuels Complex site — requires a combined licence from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, the document that authorises both construction and subsequent operation in a single proceeding. The company has pursued two paths through the NRC process, and neither has been smooth.

In January 2022, the NRC formally denied Oklo's initial Aurora licence application, citing significant information gaps in the submission. The commission found that Oklo had not provided sufficient analysis on fuel qualification methodology, the source term used to model accident scenarios, or the classification of safety systems — gaps that reflected the inherent difficulty of licensing a reactor design for which no commercial operating precedent existed in the United States. The denial was not a rejection of the Aurora concept, but it was unmistakably a reset: the company returned to pre-application engagement, restructured its submission strategy, and subsequently filed under the NRC's Part 53 framework.

Part 53, enacted through the Nuclear Energy Innovation and Modernization Act, represents a deliberate regulatory modernisation. It dispenses with light-water-reactor-centric assumptions embedded in the existing Part 50 and Part 52 rules and establishes technology-inclusive safety performance criteria intended to accommodate non-traditional designs. But the framework is new, its precedent base is thin, and NRC staff reviewing Oklo's application are, in effect, building interpretive practice as they proceed. The first Part 53 combined licence in U.S. history will be, by definition, a first.

The near-term mitigant is substantive: Oklo's resubmission benefits from structured pre-application engagement with NRC staff, including technical meetings that enter the public docket, and DOE's continued commitment to the INL demonstration site provides institutional backing that no purely private applicant can replicate. The medium-term concern is equally real. Any licence docketing, review, hearing, and issuance timeline is subject to NRC staff capacity, potential intervenor petitions, and the interpretive novelty of Part 53 itself. Historical COL reviews for Generation III-plus reactors have run four to seven years from docketing to issuance; Part 53's streamlining is untested at scale.

## HALEU: A Structural Supply Constraint

Aurora runs on high-assay low-enriched uranium — HALEU, enriched between five and twenty percent U-235 — rather than the low-enriched uranium that fuels the conventional reactor fleet. The distinction carries significant supply-chain consequences. HALEU requires dedicated enrichment cascades and handling infrastructure that did not exist at commercial scale in the United States as of the frozen snapshot date.

The 2024 Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act removed TENEX, Russia's state enricher, as a source of accessible HALEU for U.S. buyers. Centrus Energy operates a small HALEU demonstration cascade at its Piketon, Ohio, facility under a DOE contract, but production volumes are measured in kilograms per year, not the metric tons a commercial reactor fleet demands. Urenco, the Anglo-Dutch-German consortium, operates domestic enrichment capacity at its Louisiana Energy Services facility in New Mexico but requires additional capital investment to extend assay levels to HALEU specification. Neither Centrus nor Urenco had committed, on the public record available through the frozen snapshot date, to the throughput volumes required for a multi-reactor Aurora commercial programme.

The near-term mitigant is that the INL demonstration unit is a single reactor requiring a modest initial fuel load, and DOE mechanisms — including contractual support under the Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program — can backstop demonstration-scale HALEU supply. The medium-term concern is structural: the commercial case for Aurora depends on scaling from one reactor to dozens or hundreds, and no domestic HALEU supply chain capable of supporting that trajectory had been fully capitalised or contracted as of the snapshot date. Oklo's fuel pathway is thus hostage to investment decisions made by enrichers over whom it exercises no control.

## LOI-to-Revenue Conversion: The Pipeline Is Non-Binding

Oklo's commercial narrative rests in substantial part on its letter of intent pipeline. The most prominent is the [Equinix](https://investors.oklo.com) 500 MW LOI, which, when announced, represented the largest single data centre customer commitment disclosed by any SMR developer. Switch executed a separate LOI; the Wyoming Energy Authority, Diamondback Energy in the Permian Basin, and Eielson Air Force Base in Alaska completed the disclosed roster.

Each instrument is non-binding. An LOI signals intent, not obligation. Converting any LOI to a firm power purchase agreement or engineering-procurement-construction contract requires, at minimum, that Oklo obtain its NRC combined licence, secure adequate fuel supply, identify a construction site, demonstrate a credible cost and schedule, and — in most cases — permit customers to evaluate operating performance from a completed Aurora unit. That sequential prerequisite chain means that even a counterparty with genuine commercial appetite cannot convert its LOI to a binding commitment until Oklo has cleared milestones that are themselves years away.

The risk is not that the pipeline is insincere. The risk is attrition over time. Over the multi-year horizon required to clear regulatory and construction gates, customer capital allocation priorities shift, competing technology options mature, and electricity market conditions evolve. Equinix executed its LOI in a market where SMR optionality was scarce and data centre load growth had outpaced grid interconnection queues. The competitive landscape by the time Oklo is positioned to deliver power may look materially different, and LOI counterparties carry no contractual obligation to wait.

## Construction Execution: First-of-a-Kind Costs

No Aurora powerhouse has ever been built. The plant at INL, if and when licensed, will be the first of its kind — and first-of-a-kind reactor construction has a documented history of cost overruns and schedule slippage in the United States. The Vogtle 3 and 4 AP1000 units in Georgia — the most recent large reactor projects brought to commercial operation domestically — came in years late and billions over their original budgets, even employing a design that had already been completed in China.

Aurora's compact footprint and factory-module strategy represent genuine mitigants: the plant's small physical scale limits on-site civil construction scope, and factory fabrication in principle transfers quality control from the field to a controlled manufacturing environment. DeWitte has characterised the Aurora approach as a manufactured product rather than a bespoke construction project, and the design's EBR-II heritage — drawn from a reactor that accumulated roughly thirty years of operation at INL — provides a credible engineering foundation. But the INL demonstration is, by definition, not yet a manufactured product at scale. It is a prototype, and prototypes absorb prototype-scale uncertainty in cost, schedule, and first-article problem resolution.

## Capital: Pre-Revenue, Multi-Year Horizon

Oklo brought approximately $306 million of net cash onto its balance sheet at the SPAC close in May 2024, after redemptions and transaction costs. Against a multi-year path to first revenue — encompassing NRC review, fuel procurement, construction, and commissioning — that balance functions as a bridge, not a destination. The company had not disclosed a committed project finance facility or a DOE Loan Programs Office guarantee as of the frozen snapshot date that would substantially de-risk the capital cost of the first plant and the commercial fleet that must follow it.

Additional equity issuance, project debt, a government-backed loan, or some combination of all three will be required before Aurora generates revenue. Each mechanism carries cost. Equity dilutes existing shareholders at whatever price the market will support at the time of issuance; project finance for an unlicensed, unproven reactor design commands structurally wide spreads if available at all without a federal credit backstop. Oklo's listed-equity status and high-profile sponsorship give it market access that purely private developers cannot match, but the quantum and blended cost of future capital remain materially uncertain.

## Competitive Technology: The Broader SMR Field

Oklo competes, indirectly, with every advanced reactor developer pursuing the data centre and distributed industrial power market. NuScale's VOYGR light-water SMR design completed NRC design certification. TerraPower's Natrium sodium fast reactor — backed by Bill Gates, supported under DOE's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program — was under construction in Wyoming as of the snapshot date. Kairos Power's fluoride-salt-cooled design was in advanced NRC review. X-energy's pebble-bed high-temperature gas reactor carried DOE backing. BWXT Advanced Technologies was advancing microreactor designs with established defence relationships.

None of these programmes had produced commercial power at scale as of the frozen snapshot date; the SMR field as a whole remained in the demonstration phase. The competitive risk for Oklo is not primarily that a rival reaches commercial operation years ahead of it. The risk is subtler: that a rival's licensing precedent, operating data, or cost performance reshapes customer expectations and counterparty contract preferences in ways that disadvantage Oklo's specific technology profile and commercial proposition before Aurora has generated sufficient operating history to compete on its own merits.

## The Compound Probability

The investor calculus is not any single risk in isolation. It is the joint probability that NRC licensing, HALEU supply, LOI conversion, construction execution, and adequate capital all achieve favourable outcomes across a five-to-ten-year horizon, in roughly that sequence, with each gate requiring passage before the next becomes actionable. Genuine mitigants exist at every layer: DOE site access and institutional support, SPAC-funded liquidity, EBR-II design heritage, high-profile sponsorship, and a customer LOI pipeline that signals credible demand. None of those mitigants eliminates the underlying uncertainty. An investor holding Oklo equity is underwriting a sequentially gated option on a technology category that had not yet produced commercial power in the United States, with terminal value contingent on clearing every gate in order — and without the margin for error that sequential dependency, almost by definition, does not permit.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## Twelve months in a pre-revenue company

The disciplined investor arriving at Oklo's stock in the weeks surrounding the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026 confronted a familiar asymmetry: a pre-revenue, pre-permit advanced reactor developer trading almost entirely on optionality, with no quarterly earnings beats to anchor sentiment and no product shipments to validate the pipeline. The next twelve months — June 2026 through approximately May 2027 — will not change that structural fact. What they will do is resolve, or fail to resolve, the three binary questions that underpin the entire valuation: whether the NRC combined license application for the Idaho National Laboratory site advances materially toward issuance; whether the Equinix 500-megawatt letter of intent and the broader customer pipeline migrate from indicative interest to contractually binding commitments; and whether Oklo's cash runway extends at a pace consistent with reaching the permitting and construction phases without dilutive emergency capital.

## Catalyst calendar, quarter by quarter

**Q2 2026 (results expected August 2026).** The most immediate watchpoint is the NRC docket. The combined license application for the Aurora demonstration unit at the Idaho National Laboratory site entered formal review following submission, and the NRC's parallel-track environmental review — required under the National Environmental Policy Act — was generating public comment milestones that investors had begun to treat as a leading indicator of schedule credibility. An NRC staff finding that the application is sufficiently complete to proceed to the safety evaluation stage would constitute the single most de-risking event available in this window. Absent that, the August quarterly filing will be read primarily for operating expenses and cash consumption. The key number: the gross cash balance as of 30 June 2026 against the trailing quarterly burn rate, which analysts had been modeling at roughly \$25–35 million per quarter as of late 2025, reflecting R&D intensity, nuclear regulatory consulting, and the post-SPAC public-company overhead.

**Q3 2026 (results expected November 2026).** The DOE's Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program support structure and the Idaho National Laboratory site-access agreement both carry milestone-reporting obligations. A DOE milestone completion or phase-gate progress report — typically public via DOE press release — could arrive in this window and would signal whether federal co-investment remains aligned with Oklo's internal schedule. The commercial side is equally watched: any announcement of a signed power purchase agreement or definitive offtake contract with a data centre operator would represent a qualitative shift from the LOI regime under which the entire pipeline has operated since the Equinix announcement. The Wyoming Energy Authority commitment and the Diamondback Energy engagement were both at the LOI stage as of the snapshot date; either converting to a binding agreement would sharpen analyst revenue-initiation scenarios meaningfully.

**Q4 2026 (results expected February 2027).** Year-end financials provide the clearest cash-position read. The SPAC merger with AltC Acquisition Corp closed in May 2024 and deposited approximately \$306 million onto the post-merger balance sheet, net of redemptions and transaction costs. By December 2026 — thirty-one months post-close — the cumulative burn against that base is the central solvency question. If the quarterly burn has remained at the \$25–35 million range and no capital raise has intervened, the year-end 2026 cash position would be in the \$145–220 million range: adequate runway through 2028 in the bear case, materially comfortable in the bull case. Any indication of an at-the-money equity program or shelf utilisation in the year-end proxy or 8-K disclosures would be read as a dilution signal and received negatively by momentum holders.

**Q1 2027 (results expected May 2027).** The twelve-month horizon closes with a potential major NRC milestone: the completion of the staff's preliminary safety evaluation report, which in the Part 52 COLA framework marks the point at which design-specific safety findings are formally documented. For a novel sodium-cooled fast reactor with metallic fuel, this step has historically been the most technically demanding segment of the NRC review — the ground on which Oklo's original 2020 application foundered in January 2022, when the NRC cited insufficient detail on accident source terms and fuel performance data. A favourable preliminary SER finding by mid-2027 would place the first Aurora unit on a credible path to license issuance before 2030 and compress the market's probability-weighted timeline estimates significantly.

## What consensus is actually measuring

There is no traditional revenue consensus for Oklo. The company is pre-revenue and will remain so through the entire twelve-month window described above, absent a structural surprise such as an early DOE cost-sharing payment recognised as contract revenue. Analyst estimates published by the handful of sell-side desks covering the name as of the snapshot date are best understood as operating-loss and cash-burn forecasts, plus net-present-value models built around probabilistic commercial-operation date assumptions.

The central scenario embedded in consensus models as of late May 2026 assumed:

| Metric | FY 2026E | FY 2027E | Implied trajectory |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | \$0 | \$0–\$5M (DOE milestones only) | N/A |
| Operating loss | \$(100)–\$(130)M | \$(115)–\$(145)M | Expense growth as headcount scales |
| Cash at year-end | \$160–\$200M | \$40–\$90M (pre any raise) | 2028 capital need flagged |
| First commercial revenue | 2029–2031 range | — | Highly scenario-dependent |

*Sources: Oklo 10-K filings, sell-side model assumptions. Figures are consensus midpoints and subject to wide dispersion given thin analyst coverage.*

The implied operating-loss trajectory reflects the continued ramp in nuclear engineering headcount, expanded regulatory engagement, and the commercial infrastructure required to pursue the data centre pipeline. Beat versus miss in this environment is almost entirely qualitative: a quarter that produces an NRC docket advancement, a new binding customer agreement, or a DOE milestone payment is a beat regardless of the operating loss line. A quarter that adds headcount without regulatory progress while the cash balance approaches the \$100 million threshold is a miss regardless of whether the EPS loss was slightly narrower than model.

## Management guidance on record

Jacob DeWitte has consistently declined to provide a specific commercial operation date as a formal commitment, instead framing the timeline around the NRC licensing process. In a post-SPAC investor communication, DeWitte stated:

> "We've been building toward this moment for over a decade — the technology works, the fuel cycle is coherent, and the demand signal from data centre customers has never been stronger. Our job now is to execute on the licensing process and convert the pipeline into long-term contracts."

Caroline Cochran addressed the operational readiness question in subsequent public remarks:

> "The Aurora design is based on sixty years of EBR-II operating experience at Idaho National Laboratory. We're not inventing new physics — we're taking proven fast-reactor science and packaging it for the commercial power market at a scale that data centre operators and industrial customers can actually use."

Neither statement constitutes forward financial guidance in the SEC Regulation FD sense. The absence of formal guidance reflects both the pre-revenue stage and the inherent unpredictability of NRC licensing timelines, which Oklo's management has characterised as the binding constraint on commercial deployment scheduling.

## Beat and miss thresholds

A clear beat in the next twelve months looks like any one of the following: NRC staff acceptance of the combined license application as complete and the docketing of a formal review schedule; conversion of the Equinix 500-megawatt LOI to a signed power purchase agreement or definitive offtake agreement; a new DOE cost-sharing milestone payment recognised in quarterly revenues; or announcement of a second or third HALEU fuel supply agreement that addresses the structural supply-chain constraint.

A miss looks like: NRC staff issuing a request for additional information that delays the docketing review by six months or more; Equinix publicly withdrawing the LOI or redirecting its energy procurement to competing technologies; quarterly cash burn exceeding \$40 million for two consecutive quarters without a corresponding acceleration in licensing progress; or any departure of Jacob DeWitte or Caroline Cochran from their executive roles.

## The asymmetry into the next twelve months

The bull setup rests on a single structural argument: if the NRC issues a combined license for the Aurora unit at Idaho National Laboratory in the 2028–2030 window, Oklo becomes the first commercially licensed sodium-cooled fast reactor in United States history, and the Equinix 500-megawatt LOI plus the Switch and Wyoming commitments provide the forward revenue anchor for a valuation step-change that the current option-value market cap dramatically underprices. The Sam Altman sponsorship signal, while reduced in formal governance terms by his April 2025 transition from Chairman to continuing stakeholder, retains its narrative power precisely because the AI data centre electricity demand thesis has continued to intensify.

The bear setup is equally direct: pre-revenue companies with \$150–200 million of cash runway and multi-year licensing timelines in capital-intensive regulated industries are structurally exposed to dilution cycles. The NRC has rejected one Oklo application before. HALEU supply constraints are not resolved by Oklo's commercial roadmap alone. Competing SMR developers — including X-energy, Kairos Power, and the broader TerraPower pipeline — are advancing in parallel under similar federal support structures. And the Equinix 500-megawatt LOI, like all LOIs in the SMR sector, carries no binding commitment: a single data centre procurement decision could redirect that demand to alternative solutions, including grid interconnection, large-scale battery storage, or a competing nuclear developer with faster licensing execution.

The asymmetry, viewed coldly, is that the bull case requires serial execution across NRC licensing, HALEU supply, customer contract conversion, and construction financing — four sequentially dependent processes each with independent failure modes. The bear case requires only one of them to stall materially. The investor holding Oklo into mid-2027 is, in effect, holding a series of options on those four processes resolving in sequence. The next twelve months will begin to price which sequence is actually unfolding.

chapters.title: NRC milestones, Aurora-INL construction, and the 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The regulatory crucible

When the Nuclear Regulatory Commission returned Oklo's first combined licence application in January 2022, the company had been four years into an effort to licence a 1.5-megawatt Aurora plant at the Idaho National Laboratory — a milestone that would have made it the first advanced non-light-water reactor to receive NRC authorisation since the 1970s. The agency identified insufficient analysis of potential accident scenarios and inadequate information on the reactor's safety framework. It was a corrective rather than a condemnation: the NRC did not hold that Aurora was unlicensable, only that the submission as filed did not meet the evidentiary threshold. But the setback reset the timeline by years and reinforced a structural reality about nuclear regulation in the United States — pre-application engagement is as consequential as the formal filing itself.

## The Part 53 pathway

By the time Oklo completed its merger with AltC Acquisition Corp in May 2024, the regulatory landscape had shifted in the company's favour. The NRC's Part 53 rulemaking — a framework designed specifically for advanced, non-light-water reactor designs that cannot be evaluated through prescriptive Part 52 light-water standards — had advanced substantially. Part 53 allows applicants to propose technology-inclusive safety performance criteria rather than prescriptive specifications inherited from legacy pressurised-water and boiling-water reactor rules. For Oklo, whose Aurora powerhouse operates as a fast-spectrum sodium-cooled metallic-fuel reactor with passive safety characteristics derived from the Experimental Breeder Reactor II lineage at Idaho National Laboratory, the prescriptive legacy framework was a structural misfit. Part 53 provides the appropriate evaluation pathway.

Pre-application engagement with NRC staff was sustained through 2025 and into 2026, covering Aurora's safety case, accident-source-term methodology, and passive shutdown characteristics. The company's stated target is a renewed combined licence application under the advanced reactor framework, with a staff technical review leading to an Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards hearing and ultimately an NRC board decision within the first half of the decade. No binding decision date has been publicly disclosed. The NRC's own schedule is contingent on the volume and completeness of the application package and on agency staffing capacity — factors outside Oklo's control.

## Aurora-INL: the demonstration imperative

The Idaho National Laboratory site remains the nominated location for Aurora's first commercial-scale deployment. The DOE granted Oklo a site use permit at INL, and the two organisations maintain a partnership aligned with the agency's interest in demonstrating advanced reactor technology at a national laboratory site. INL's proximity to decades of fast-reactor operational data — EBR-II operated there from 1964 to 1994 — provides both technical and institutional continuity.

Oklo's publicly stated target is commercial operation of the Aurora-INL plant by the late 2020s, with an internal planning horizon of approximately 2030. That target is conditional on a positive NRC combined licence decision no later than 2027-2028, which would allow construction commencement while remaining regulatory steps are still proceeding in parallel. Construction of even a compact 15-to-75-megawatt plant of novel fast-reactor design at a federally managed site involves material schedule exposure. Nuclear construction programmes in the United States have consistently run behind initial projections — a pattern the industry has not solved at scale.

## HALEU: the fuel-chain constraint

Aurora's dependence on high-assay low-enriched uranium — enriched to between five and twenty percent U-235 — constitutes the most structurally embedded risk in Oklo's operating plan. Prior to Congressional action restricting Russian uranium imports, Russia's TENEX subsidiary had been the principal commercially available HALEU source. The Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act, enacted in 2024, removed that pathway, transferring the supply question entirely to domestic enrichment capacity.

The only US facility capable of producing commercial HALEU as of 2026 is Centrus Energy's American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio, which operates a twelve-centrifuge demonstration cascade under DOE contract. Output is measured in kilograms per year — insufficient to fuel even a single Aurora plant at commercial scale without substantial expansion. DOE's broader HALEU availability programme has provided cost-share funding to accelerate domestic enrichment. But the gap between planned capacity and Aurora's first-plant fuel requirements remains wide on a two-to-three-year horizon. Oklo has cited its Aurora fuel cycle — which incorporates recycled spent fuel from fast-reactor operations — as a structural mitigant to long-term HALEU demand. The initial fuel loading of a first plant still requires fresh HALEU supply, a dependency the company shares with TerraPower's Natrium programme, which disclosed HALEU-related construction delays of its own.

## Converting the LOI pipeline

The customer letter-of-intent pipeline assembled between 2021 and 2025 is the commercial architecture on which Oklo's equity story rests. The Equinix 500-megawatt LOI, the largest single data-centre SMR commitment disclosed by any developer in the industry, attracted sustained institutional attention. Switch's LOI, the Wyoming Energy Authority engagement, the Eielson Air Force Base demonstration selection, and Diamondback Energy's Permian Basin interest collectively sketch a customer base spanning hyperscale data-centre operators, defence deployments, and industrial off-grid applications.

Converting LOIs to definitive power purchase agreements requires, as a prerequisite, a credible NRC licence timeline. Data-centre operators making multi-year capital allocation decisions cannot contract to capacity that carries no licence or construction schedule. As of May 2026, no Oklo LOI had converted to a binding power purchase agreement. The Equinix 500 megawatts, at a notional $80-per-megawatt-hour offtake rate across a ten-year term, would represent a contract value in excess of $3.5 billion — a figure that would transform Oklo's financial profile but remains entirely prospective.

## Capital requirements

Oklo entered the post-merger period with approximately $306 million in cash following the May 2024 AltC transaction, net of redemptions and transaction costs. Against an annual burn rate reflecting research, development, and NRC-related regulatory expenditure, that balance extends the company's runway well into the late 2020s at current spending levels. First-plant construction is a different order of magnitude. Industry estimates for a first-of-kind advanced reactor at a national laboratory site — incorporating engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning, and contingency — range from $400 million to upward of $1 billion for a plant in the 15-to-75-megawatt range, with first-of-kind cost premiums that are structurally difficult to model in advance.

Oklo will require a substantial capital raise, most likely a combination of equity issuance and project-level debt or DOE Loan Programs Office support, to fund Aurora-INL construction. A dilutive equity raise at a critical point in the regulatory timeline is a risk that existing shareholders have priced but not resolved.

## The competitive field

The SMR developer landscape has contracted and stratified since 2022.

| Developer | Design | Status (May 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| NuScale Power | 77 MWe LWR module | UAMPS project cancelled Nov 2023; design certified; seeking customers |
| TerraPower | 345 MW Natrium (Na-cooled) | Construction underway, Kemmerer WY; HALEU-related delays |
| Kairos Power | 140 MWt KP-FHR (FLiBe salt) | Hermes demo plant under construction, Oak Ridge TN |
| X-energy | 80 MWe Xe-100 (pebble bed) | ARDP project with Dow; pre-construction phase |
| BWXT | Microreactor (Project Pele) | DoD-focused; mobile prototype testing |
| **Oklo** | **15–75 MWe Aurora (Na-cooled)** | **NRC pre-application; INL site; LOI pipeline** |

NuScale's November 2023 cancellation of the Carbon Free Power Project — driven by per-megawatt cost estimates that rose above $89 per megawatt-hour — recalibrated investor expectations for SMR timelines and economics across the sector. TerraPower's Natrium programme, backed by Breakthrough Energy Ventures and a substantial DOE ARDP award, represents the most advanced non-light-water construction effort in the US as of mid-2026, despite its own HALEU delays. Kairos Power's Hermes demonstration at Oak Ridge — a non-power heat plant using fluoride salt coolant and TRISO fuel — represents the most rapidly licensed advanced reactor effort in the current NRC pipeline. Against this field, Oklo's differentiation is its sodium fast-reactor heritage, the smaller-footprint modular configurations designed for distributed data-centre deployment, and the commercial signal embedded in Sam Altman's continued board chairmanship.

## The central question

Whether Oklo translates its customer LOI pipeline, its DOE partnership, and its equity market positioning into a completed NRC combined licence, an Aurora-INL construction start, and first commercial operation before 2031 depends on the resolution of a chain of dependencies that do not individually sit within management's control. The NRC process is autonomous. The HALEU supply chain requires federal investment and private enrichment expansion that will take years. LOI conversion is contingent on licensing credibility. Construction execution at a federally managed site is subject to regulatory, labour, and supply chain variables that project management cannot eliminate.

What Oklo has assembled — the INL site agreement, the DOE partnership, the largest data-centre LOI in the SMR industry, a public equity base derived from a $850 million SPAC-implied valuation, and the institutional credibility of Altman's association — is the most credible foundation available to a pre-revenue fast-reactor developer in the current US nuclear renaissance. The company entered 2026 with the NRC engagement live, the INL site secured, and a customer pipeline that, if converted, would make Aurora the defining energy infrastructure investment of the AI data-centre build-out. The distance between that foundation and a commissioned plant remained, as of May 2026, a multi-year journey across regulatory, fuel-supply, capital, and construction terrain that no developer in this technology class had yet traversed in the modern US regulatory environment. The thesis was intact. The proof of concept had not yet been built.

## Appendix C — Aurora Technology Summary

The Aurora powerhouse is a compact fast-spectrum sodium-cooled reactor drawing direct design heritage from the Experimental Breeder Reactor II (EBR-II), operated by Argonne National Laboratory at Idaho National Laboratory from 1964 to 1994. The metallic fuel design enables passive safety shutdown characteristics without active cooling intervention. Three nominal plant configurations have been disclosed: 15 MW, 50 MW, and 75 MW electric output — each smaller than NuScale's 77 MW SMR module and substantially below traditional 1,000 MW-class Generation III+ reactors, positioning Aurora for distributed deployment at industrial and data-centre sites.

Fuel feed is high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU), enriched above 5 percent but below 20 percent U-235. Oklo's roadmap incorporates the use of recycled spent fuel from legacy research reactors as a supplemental feed source. HALEU supply remains structurally constrained as of the snapshot date, with US domestic enrichment capacity limited following the statutory ban on Russian-origin enriched uranium.
